title: Explain Section 174 amortization changes for 2024
description: For 2024, U.S. businesses had to capitalize specified research expenditures, amortizing domestic costs over five years and foreign costs over 15 years.
summary: Section 174 amortization changes for 2024: U.S. businesses had to capitalize 2024 specified research or experimental expenditures, amortizing domestic costs over five years and foreign costs over 15 years from the taxable-year midpoint. 2024 was the final mandatory domestic capitalization year; Public Law 119-21 now lets taxpayers deduct remaining unamortized 2022–2024 domestic balances in 2025 or ratably over 2025–2026.

body.text: Section 174 amortization changes for 2024: U.S. businesses had to capitalize 2024 specified research or experimental expenditures, amortizing domestic costs over five years and foreign costs over 15 years from the taxable-year midpoint. 2024 was the final mandatory domestic capitalization year; Public Law 119-21 now lets taxpayers deduct remaining unamortized 2022–2024 domestic balances in 2025 or ratably over 2025–2026.

This report provides a comprehensive statutory and procedural analysis of the Section 174 capitalization and amortization regime as it governed the 2024 tax year, alongside the transition, acceleration, and retroactive recovery rules enacted under Public Law 119-21.

Scope note. This report covers the federal and state income tax rules governing the capitalization and amortization of specified research or experimental (SRE) expenditures under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 174 through the 2024 tax year, as well as how subsequent legislative enactments in 2025 and administrative procedures in 2025 and 2026 altered the recovery of 2024 and prior-vintage expenditures.
1. Why 2024 matters: the last year of mandatory capitalization
1.1 The pre-2022 baseline

Internal Revenue Code Section 174 was originally enacted on August 16, 1954, as part of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954 (ch. 736, 68A Stat. 66). For nearly seven decades prior to the effective date of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) amendments, former Section 174 provided taxpayers with a flexible statutory framework for recovering research or experimental (R&E) expenditures paid or incurred in connection with a trade or business. Under former Section 174(a)(1), a taxpayer could elect to treat research or experimental expenditures that were not chargeable to a depreciable or depletable property account as current expenses and deduct them in full in the taxable year in which they were paid or incurred. Once adopted, this current-expense method applied to all research or experimental expenditures regularly paid or incurred by the taxpayer unless the taxpayer obtained the consent of the Secretary of the Treasury (acting through the Commissioner of Internal Revenue) to change to a different method for all or part of such expenditures under former Section 174(a)(3).

Alternatively, under former Section 174(b)(1), a taxpayer could elect to treat research or experimental expenditures that were chargeable to a capital account—but not chargeable to property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation under Section 167 or depletion under Section 611—as deferred expenses. Where a taxpayer made a valid election under former Section 174(b), those deferred expenditures were amortized ratably over a period selected by the taxpayer of not less than 60 consecutive months, beginning with the month in which the taxpayer first realized benefits from the expenditures. Under former Section 174(b)(1), expenditures treated as deferred expenses were explicitly deemed to be expenditures properly chargeable to capital account for purposes of Section 1016(a)(1), thereby increasing the adjusted basis of the resulting property. Furthermore, the statutory cross-references in former Section 174(f) directed taxpayers to Section 1016(a)(14) regarding required downward adjustments to property basis for amounts allowed as deductions under Section 174(b), and to Section 59(e) regarding the optional 10-year ratable write-off available to taxpayers seeking to avoid alternative minimum tax (AMT) preference adjustments on otherwise currently deductible Section 174(a) expenditures. From a tax-policy and analytical standpoint, practitioners and legal commentators (including analyses published in Tax Notes) have observed that these interrelated basis adjustment rules under Section 1016(a)(1) and Section 1016(a)(14), combined with the "first realizes benefits" amortization trigger, conceptually treated deferred R&E expenditures similarly to self-created intangible assets under Treasury Regulation Section 1.263(a)-4, even though that conceptual analogy represents tax commentary rather than an independent rule of substantive law.
1.2 The TCJA mandate and its effective date

On December 22, 2017, Congress enacted Public Law 115-97 (131 Stat. 2054), commonly known as the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA). Section 13206(a) of Public Law 115-97 fundamentally rewrote Section 174 on a delayed effective-date schedule. Rather than permitting taxpayers to choose between immediate current expensing and elective 60-month deferral upon the realization of benefits, TCJA-amended Section 174(a)(1) established a strict statutory prohibition stating that no current deduction is allowed for "specified research or experimental expenditures" (SRE expenditures). Instead, TCJA Section 174(a)(2) mandated that taxpayers charge all specified research or experimental expenditures to a capital account and amortize them ratably over fixed statutory recovery periods.

Pursuant to Section 13206(e) of Public Law 115-97, this mandatory capitalization and amortization regime took effect for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021. Under Section 13206(b) of Public Law 115-97, the transition from pre-TCJA Section 174 to TCJA-amended Section 174 was statutorily designated as a change in method of accounting initiated by the taxpayer under Section 446(e), made with the automatic consent of the Secretary of the Treasury, and applied strictly on a cut-off basis only to specified research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021. Because the statute mandated a cut-off transition, no adjustment under Section 481(a) was permitted or required for research or experimental costs incurred in taxable years beginning before January 1, 2022.

For a calendar-year taxpayer, the mandatory capitalization rules of TCJA Section 174 governed the 2022, 2023, and 2024 tax years. Consequently, 2024 was the final tax year in which domestic specified research or experimental expenditures were subject to mandatory capitalization and 5-year amortization, because the subsequent restoration of domestic expensing under Section 174A (enacted by Public Law 119-21 on July 4, 2025) applies prospectively to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024 (subject to specific transition and small-business retroactive elections detailed in Section 3 of this report). While numerous tax practitioners and industry groups anticipated between 2018 and 2021 that Congress would repeal or defer Section 13206 of the TCJA prior to its January 1, 2022 trigger date, no pre-effective-date legislative deferral was enacted, and the TCJA capitalization mandate operated in full force throughout the 2022–2024 window.

body.text: 2. The amortization rules that governed 2024 expenditures
2.1 Recovery periods and the midpoint convention

Under TCJA Section 174(a)(2)(B), specified research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred during the 2024 tax year had to be capitalized and amortized ratably over a 5-year period (60 months) in the case of domestic research, or over a 15-year period (180 months) in the case of foreign research. Under Section 174(a)(2)(B)(ii), "foreign research" is defined by cross-reference to Section 41(d)(4)(F) as any research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any territory or possession of the United States. Thus, the geographic location where the physical research and experimental activities are performed—rather than the tax residence of the entity paying for the research or the legal jurisdiction where resulting intellectual property is registered—determines whether an expenditure is subject to the 5-year domestic schedule or the 15-year foreign schedule.

Critically, TCJA Section 174(a)(2)(B) mandated that the amortization period begin at the midpoint of the taxable year in which the specified research or experimental expenditures are paid or incurred. In Notice 2023-63, Section 3.05, the IRS clarified that for a standard 12-month taxable year, the midpoint is the first day of the seventh month of the taxable year (July 1 for a calendar-year taxpayer). For short taxable years consisting of fewer than 12 months, Notice 2023-63 provides specific month-and-day conventions to establish the exact midpoint. This statutory midpoint convention applies mechanically to all SRE expenditures paid or incurred during the taxable year, regardless of whether a specific cost was actually incurred in January, July, or December.
The arithmetic consequence of the midpoint convention is substantial in the initial year of expenditure:

items: Domestic SRE expenditures: For a calendar-year taxpayer incurring domestic SRE costs in 2024, only six months of amortization (July through December) out of the 60-month recovery schedule could be deducted on the 2024 return. This equals exactly 10% of the 2024 domestic SRE expenditures (6 ÷ 60 = 10%). The remaining 90% remained capitalized at the close of 2024, scheduled under the baseline TCJA rules to be recovered at 20% per year in 2025, 2026, 2027, and 2028 (12 ÷ 60 = 20% each year), with the final 10% (6 ÷ 60 = 10%) recovered in the first half of 2029.

Foreign SRE expenditures: For a calendar-year taxpayer incurring foreign SRE costs in 2024, only six months out of the 180-month recovery schedule could be deducted in 2024, yielding a year-one deduction of 3.33% (6 ÷ 180 = 3.333%). Thereafter, 6.67% (12 ÷ 180) is deductible in each of the 14 full calendar years from 2025 through 2038, with the final 3.33% (6 ÷ 180) deductible in 2039.

body.text: 2.2 What had to be capitalized

TCJA Section 174(b) defined "specified research or experimental expenditures" as research or experimental expenditures (within the meaning of Treasury Regulation Section 1.174-2) that are paid or incurred by the taxpayer during the taxable year in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business. The scope of capitalization for the 2024 tax year encompassed several critical statutory and administrative rules:

items: Software development. Under TCJA Section 174(c)(3), any amount paid or incurred in connection with the development of any software is statutorily treated as a research or experimental expenditure. Consequently, software development costs—whether incurred to create software for sale or licensing to third parties, software embedded in hardware, or internal-use software (such as enterprise resource planning upgrades or SaaS platform architecture)—were automatically swept into mandatory Section 174 capitalization. To align administrative guidance with this statutory mandate, IRS Notice 2023-63 (Section 12) and Notice 2024-12 formally declared Section 5 of Revenue Procedure 2000-50 obsolete for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021. Under Notice 2023-63, Section 5, activities treated as software development include planning the development of software, designing the software or upgrades and enhancements, building a model, writing and converting source code, and testing the software to eliminate defects prior to commercial release or internal placement in service, whereas routine post-deployment maintenance that does not give rise to upgrades or enhancements remains deductible.

Exhaustive cost categories vs. excluded overhead. In Notice 2023-63, Section 4.03(1), the IRS provided an exhaustive list of cost categories that must be capitalized as SRE expenditures when paid or incurred in the performance of SRE activities or in the direct support of SRE activities:

Labor costs: All elements of compensation (including basic compensation, stock-based compensation, overtime, vacation, sick leave, payroll taxes, and pension costs, but specifically excluding severance pay) for full-time, part-time, and contract employees and independent contractors to the extent they perform, supervise, or directly support SRE activities.

Materials and supplies costs: Costs of materials, supplies, and tools or equipment that are not depreciable under Section 167 and that are used or consumed in the performance or direct support of SRE activities.

Cost recovery allowances: Depreciation, amortization, or depletion allowances with respect to property used in the performance or direct support of SRE activities, allocated in proportion to the property's use in SRE activities.
Patent costs: Costs incurred in obtaining a patent, such as attorneys' fees expended in making and perfecting a patent application.

Certain operation and management costs: Rent, utilities, insurance, taxes, repairs and maintenance, security, and similar overhead costs with respect to facilities, equipment, and other assets used in the performance or direct support of SRE activities.
Travel costs: Travel expenditures incurred for the performance or direct support of SRE activities.

body.text: While non-authoritative summaries sometimes characterize Section 174 as capturing a "sweeping array of allocable overhead," Notice 2023-63, Section 4.03(2), explicitly narrows this reach by excluding indirect general and administrative (G&A) service department costs (such as human resources, payroll, accounting, corporate legal, and executive management departments that only indirectly benefit research activities), interest on debt incurred to finance SRE activities, website hosting costs, and amortization of pre-2022 R&E costs. Under Notice 2023-63, Section 4.03(3), taxpayers must allocate mixed costs between SRE and non-SRE activities on the basis of a cause-and-effect relationship or another reasonable method applied consistently.

items: Independence from the Section 41 research credit. Mandatory capitalization under Section 174 applies to all SRE expenditures regardless of whether the taxpayer claims or qualifies for the research credit under Section 41. Notice 2023-63, Section 1, expressly confirms that the guidance governing Section 174 does not alter the rules for determining eligibility for, or calculating the amount of, the Section 41 credit. Because Section 41 Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) are limited to direct in-house wages, direct supplies, computer rental costs, and 65% (or 75%/100% for certain consortia and eligible contractors) of contract research expenses, a taxpayer's Section 174 SRE expenditure base (which includes facilities overhead, depreciation, patent legal fees, and 100% of qualifying contract research) is substantially broader than its Section 41 QRE base.

Absence of a de minimis exception. Neither TCJA-amended Section 174 nor the interim administrative framework in Notice 2023-63 and Notice 2024-12 provides any de minimis dollar threshold or small-taxpayer exemption during the 2022–2024 statutory window (prior to the retroactive small-business election enacted in 2025).

body.text: 2.3 Dispositions, retirements and abandonments

Under TCJA Section 174(d), if any property with respect to which specified research or experimental expenditures are paid or incurred is disposed of, retired, or abandoned during the 5-year or 15-year amortization period, no deduction is allowed with respect to such expenditures on account of that disposition, retirement, or abandonment, and the amortization deduction must continue over the remainder of the original statutory period.

In Notice 2023-63, Section 7, the IRS confirmed that this "stranded amortization" rule applies strictly even if the underlying research project fails and is abandoned prior to the midpoint of the taxable year in which the costs were incurred. Furthermore, if property developed through SRE activities is sold in a taxable transaction during the amortization period, the taxpayer cannot use the unamortized SRE balance to offset the amount realized or accelerate the deduction at closing; the transferor must continue amortizing the remaining SRE balance on its own tax returns over the original 60-month or 180-month schedule. Notice 2023-63, Section 7.04(2), provides a narrow exception only where a corporation completely ceases to exist in a transaction not described in Section 381(a) (such as a complete taxable liquidation under Section 331), allowing the terminating corporation to deduct its remaining unamortized SRE expenditures in its final taxable year unless a principal purpose of the transaction is to claim the accelerated deduction.
2.4 Interim guidance and accounting method change procedures for 2022–2024
To administer TCJA Section 174 during the 2022–2024 tax years, the Treasury Department and the IRS issued a series of administrative notices and automatic accounting method change revenue procedures:

items: Notice 2023-63 and Notice 2024-12 (Substantive Interim Rules): Issued on September 8, 2023, Notice 2023-63 (2023-39 I.R.B. 919) set forth comprehensive substantive rules that the Treasury Department and the IRS announced they intended to incorporate into forthcoming proposed regulations, addressing the midpoint convention (Section 3), the scope and allocation of SRE expenditures (Section 4), software development (Section 5), research performed under contract (Section 6), dispositions, retirements, and abandonments (Section 7), long-term contracts under Section 460 (Section 8), and cost-sharing arrangements under Section 482 (Section 9). On December 22, 2023, the IRS issued Notice 2024-12 (2024-5 I.R.B. 616), which modified and clarified Notice 2023-63 in two vital respects:

Selective reliance permitted: Notice 2024-12 removed the "all-or-nothing" reliance condition, allowing taxpayers to rely on selected sections of Notice 2023-63 (Sections 3 through 9) without being forced to adopt every section, provided the taxpayer applies the chosen section(s) in their entirety in a consistent manner.

Relief for contract research providers: Notice 2024-12 clarified Section 6 of Notice 2023-63 by establishing that if a research provider performs research under contract for a third party, bears no financial risk under the contract, and obtains only an "excluded SRE product right" (meaning an incidental right to use the resulting SRE product that is either separately bargained for or acquired solely to perform the contract research), the research provider's costs are not treated as SRE expenditures subject to Section 174 capitalization.

body.text: Subsequently, Revenue Procedure 2025-28, Section 7.01, and Revenue Procedure 2026-32 confirmed that taxpayers may continue to rely on Sections 3 through 7 of Notice 2023-63 (as modified by Notice 2024-12) for SRE expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning before January 1, 2025 (and for foreign research expenditures thereafter).

items: Procedural Revenue Procedures and Audit Protection for 2024: Changes in a taxpayer's treatment of SRE expenditures to comply with TCJA Section 174 or to rely on Notice 2023-63 / Notice 2024-12 were administered through the automatic accounting method change procedures under Revenue Procedure 2015-13, as successively modified by Revenue Procedure 2023-8, Revenue Procedure 2023-11, Revenue Procedure 2024-9, Revenue Procedure 2024-23 (Section 7.01, Designated Automatic Accounting Method Change Number 265), Revenue Procedure 2024-34, and Revenue Procedure 2025-8 (2025-3 I.R.B. 418, issued December 17, 2024).

body.text: Under earlier procedural guidance (Revenue Procedure 2024-23, Section 7.01(6), as modified by Revenue Procedure 2024-34), the IRS denied audit protection under Section 8.01 of Revenue Procedure 2015-13 for an automatic Section 174 method change made for a taxable year beginning in 2022 or 2023 if the taxpayer had failed to make a Section 174 method change for its first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2021. However, Revenue Procedure 2025-8 explicitly modified Section 7.01(5) and Section 7.01(6) of Revenue Procedure 2024-23 for taxable years beginning in 2024. Specifically, Revenue Procedure 2025-8 (1) waived the 5-year prior-change eligibility limitation of Section 5.01(1)(f) and the final-year-of-trade-or-business limitation of Section 5.01(1)(d) of Revenue Procedure 2015-13 so that taxpayers could file successive automatic changes on Form 3115 for a taxable year beginning in 2024 regardless of prior Section 174 method changes in 2022 or 2023, and (2) did not extend the audit protection denial to 2024. Consequently, under Revenue Procedure 2025-8, a taxpayer filing an automatic Section 174 accounting method change (Designated Change Number 265) for a taxable year beginning in 2024 does receive standard audit protection under Section 8.01 of Revenue Procedure 2015-13 with respect to pre-2024 taxable years (meaning the IRS will not require the taxpayer on exam to change its method for the same item for a taxable year prior to 2024, though audit protection never applies to pre-2022 expenditures).

body.text: 2.5 Worked example A (hypothetical): costs paid in calendar 2024

Assume a calendar-year corporate taxpayer pays $1,000,000 of domestic SRE expenditures and $300,000 of foreign SRE expenditures during calendar year 2024. Under the baseline TCJA Section 174 amortization schedules (prior to applying any 2025 transition acceleration or retroactive small-business election), the annual amortization deductions are calculated as follows:

cells: 2029 (final half year for domestic; full year for foreign)

body.text: At the close of December 31, 2024, the taxpayer holds an unamortized domestic SRE capital balance of $900,000 ($1,000,000 less the $100,000 2024 deduction). That $900,000 unamortized domestic balance is eligible for the accelerated 1-year or 2-year recovery elections enacted in 2025 (see Section 3.2). Conversely, the unamortized foreign SRE capital balance of $290,000 ($300,000 less the $10,000 2024 deduction) receives no transition relief and remains locked into its 15-year recovery schedule through 2039.
3. How the 2025 legislation changed the treatment of 2024 and earlier amounts
3.1 The new framework (taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024)

On July 4, 2025, Congress enacted Public Law 119-21, officially titled the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) and also referred to in IRS public communications as the Working Families Tax Cuts. Section 70302 of Public Law 119-21 fundamentally restructured the statutory treatment of research and experimental expenditures by adding Section 174A ("Domestic research or experimental expenditures") to the Internal Revenue Code and narrowing Section 174 exclusively to foreign research or experimental expenditures:

items: Immediate expensing of domestic R&E (§174A(a)): Pursuant to Section 174A(a), notwithstanding Section 263, there is allowed as a current deduction any "domestic research or experimental expenditures" (defined in Section 174A(b) as research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred by the taxpayer in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business other than foreign research within the meaning of Section 41(d)(4)(F)) paid or incurred during the taxable year. Section 174A contains no statutory sunset date, making permanent domestic R&E expensing the default rule for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024.

Elective capitalization of domestic R&E (§174A(c) and §59(e)): Under Section 174A(c), in lieu of deducting domestic R&E expenditures currently under Section 174A(a), a taxpayer may elect to charge such expenditures to a capital account and amortize them ratably over a period selected by the taxpayer of not less than 60 months, beginning with the month in which the taxpayer first realizes benefits from such expenditures. Under Section 174A(c)(2), this election must be made not later than the time prescribed by law for filing the return for the taxable year (including extensions) and applies to all subsequent taxable years unless the Secretary consents to a change. Alternatively, under amended Section 59(e)(2)(B), a taxpayer may elect a 10-year ratable write-off for any expenditure that would otherwise be allowable as a current deduction under Section 174A(a).

Software development (§174A(d)(3)): Section 174A(d) sets forth special exclusions and inclusions: Section 174A(d)(1) excludes expenditures for land or depreciable/depletable property, Section 174A(d)(2) excludes mineral and oil/gas exploration expenditures, and Section 174A(d)(3) explicitly mandates that "for purposes of this section, any amount paid or incurred in connection with the development of any software shall be treated as a research or experimental expenditure." Thus, both Section 174A(d)(3) (for domestic software development) and Section 174(c)(3) (for foreign software development) retain the TCJA statutory rule classifying software development as R&E, keeping Section 5 of Revenue Procedure 2000-50 obsolete while allowing domestic software development costs to be immediately deducted under Section 174A(a) starting in 2025.

Continued 15-year amortization for foreign R&E (§174): Section 70302(b) of Public Law 119-21 amended Section 174 so that it applies solely to "foreign research or experimental expenditures." Foreign R&E costs must continue to be capitalized and amortized ratably over a 15-year period (180 months) beginning with the midpoint of the taxable year in which they are paid or incurred.

Strengthened disposition bar for foreign R&E (§174(d)): What Section 70302(b)(1)(C)(ii) of Public Law 119-21 did was (1) narrow Section 174(d) to foreign research or experimental expenditures, and (2) insert the phrase "or reduction to amount realized" into Section 174(d), so that no deduction or reduction to amount realized is allowed on account of the disposition, retirement, or abandonment of property connected to foreign R&E expenditures. Pursuant to Section 70302(e)(2) of Public Law 119-21, this specific amendment adding "or reduction to amount realized" applies to property disposed of, retired, or abandoned after May 12, 2025 (with a statutory "no inference" clause as to prior law).

Accounting method change mechanics (§70302(e)(3), Rev. Proc. 2025-28, and Rev. Proc. 2026-32): Under Section 70302(e)(3) of Public Law 119-21, switching from TCJA Section 174 capitalization to Section 174A current expensing for the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024, is treated as a taxpayer-initiated change in method of accounting made with the consent of the Secretary and applied on a cut-off basis with no Section 481(a) adjustment (though for a short taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024, and ending before July 4, 2025, a modified cut-off basis applies). Under Revenue Procedure 2025-28 (modifying Revenue Procedure 2025-23, Section 7.02, Designated Automatic Accounting Method Change Number 273), a taxpayer making this change for its first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024, may do so via a simplified statement attached to its return in lieu of filing Form 3115, whereas method changes made in subsequent years require Form 3115 and a modified Section 481(a) adjustment taking into account only post-2024 domestic R&E expenditures.

body.text: 3.2 Unamortized domestic amounts from 2022–2024

Crucially for taxpayers that capitalized domestic SRE expenditures in 2022, 2023, and 2024, Section 70302(f)(2) of Public Law 119-21 enacted a dedicated transition recovery election for unamortized domestic Section 174 balances. Under Section 70302(f)(2)(A), any taxpayer (regardless of gross receipts size) that charged domestic specified research or experimental expenditures to a capital account for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025, may elect to:

items: One-year full recovery (§70302(f)(2)(A)(i)): Deduct the entire remaining unamortized domestic balance in full in the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024 (calendar year 2025 for a calendar-year taxpayer); OR

Two-year ratable recovery (§70302(f)(2)(A)(ii)): Deduct the remaining unamortized domestic balance ratably (50% per year) over the 2-taxable-year period beginning with the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024 (calendar years 2025 and 2026 for a calendar-year taxpayer).

body.text: If a taxpayer makes neither election under Section 70302(f)(2), its unamortized 2022, 2023, and 2024 domestic SRE balances simply continue to amortize along their original 60-month midpoint schedules (through 2027, 2028, and 2029, respectively). Under Section 70302(f)(2)(B) and Revenue Procedure 2025-28, Section 7.02 (Designated Change Number 273), electing the 1-year or 2-year accelerated recovery of unamortized 2022–2024 domestic costs is treated as an automatic change in method of accounting applied on a cut-off basis with no Section 481(a) adjustment, implemented by attaching a required transition statement to the taxpayer's timely filed (including extensions) federal income tax return for the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024. This acceleration election applies solely to domestic R&E balances; unamortized 2022–2024 foreign R&E balances are excluded.

Strategic tax-modeling consideration: Because electing to deduct the remaining 90% of 2024 domestic R&E costs (along with the remaining 70% of 2023 costs and 50% of 2022 costs) either entirely in 2025 or ratably across 2025 and 2026 substantially reduces taxable income in those years, taxpayers must evaluate collateral interactions with taxable-income-sensitive provisions—such as the Section 163(j) business interest expense limitation, the Section 250 foreign-derived deduction eligible income (FDDEI) deduction, net operating loss (NOL) 80% absorption limits under Section 172, and Base Erosion and Anti-Abuse Tax (BEAT) thresholds under Section 59A—before selecting between the 1-year acceleration, the 2-year ratable acceleration, or continuing the 5-year TCJA schedule.
3.3 Worked example B (hypothetical): three years of unamortized domestic costs

Assume a calendar-year company paid $1,000,000 of domestic SRE expenditures in each of calendar years 2022, 2023, and 2024 ($3,000,000 cumulative domestic spend across the three TCJA capitalization years). At January 1, 2025, the taxpayer's cumulative amortization taken and remaining unamortized balance are:

In addition to deducting 100% of any new 2025 domestic R&E costs under Section 174A(a), the taxpayer has three mutually exclusive choices for recovering the $2,100,000 of unamortized 2022–2024 domestic costs (which includes the $900,000 unamortized balance from 2024):

items: Option 1 — Continue the baseline TCJA schedule: No Section 70302(f)(2) election is made. The taxpayer deducts $600,000 in 2025 ($200,000 from each of the 2022, 2023, and 2024 vintages), $600,000 in 2026, $500,000 in 2027 ($100,000 final half-year from 2022 plus $200,000 each from 2023 and 2024), $300,000 in 2028 ($100,000 final half-year from 2023 plus $200,000 from 2024), and $100,000 in 2029 (final half-year from 2024).

Option 2 — One-year full recovery election (§70302(f)(2)(A)(i)): The taxpayer elects to deduct the entire $2,100,000 unamortized balance on its 2025 federal income tax return, reducing remaining unamortized balances to $0 for 2026 and later years.

Option 3 — Two-year ratable recovery election (§70302(f)(2)(A)(ii)): The taxpayer elects to deduct $1,050,000 ($2,100,000 ÷ 2) on its 2025 return and $1,050,000 on its 2026 return, reducing remaining unamortized balances to $0 for 2027 and later years.

body.text: 3.4 Small business taxpayers: retroactive application to 2022–2024

Under Section 70302(f)(1) of Public Law 119-21 and Section 3 of Revenue Procedure 2025-28, Congress provided an exclusive retroactive election allowing an "eligible taxpayer" to apply Section 174A (immediate domestic R&E expensing or elective Section 174A(c) amortization) retroactively back to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021—thereby wiping out mandatory TCJA capitalization for the 2022, 2023, and 2024 tax years.

items: Small business eligibility and the $31,000,000 controlled-group gross receipts test: Under Section 70302(f)(1)(B) and Revenue Procedure 2025-28, Section 3.02(1), an "eligible taxpayer" is any taxpayer (other than a tax shelter prohibited from using the cash method under Section 448(a)(3)) that meets the gross receipts test of Section 448(c) for its first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024. Pursuant to Revenue Procedure 2024-40 and Revenue Procedure 2025-28, Section 3.02(1), a taxpayer meets the Section 448(c) gross receipts test for a taxable year beginning in 2025 if its average annual gross receipts for the three prior taxable years (i.e., 2022, 2023, and 2024 for a calendar-year taxpayer) do not exceed $31,000,000.

body.text: Under Section 448(c)(2) and Treasury Regulation Section 1.448-2(c)(2)(ii), all persons treated as a single employer under Section 52(a) or (b) (which incorporates parent-subsidiary, brother-sister, and combined controlled groups of corporations under Section 1563(a) and trades or businesses under common control under Treasury Regulation Section 1.52-1) or Section 414(m) or (o) (affiliated service groups) must be treated as one person for purposes of the Section 448(c) gross receipts test. Therefore, gross receipts of all controlled-group and common-control entities are mandatorily aggregated when determining whether the $31,000,000 threshold is met.

items: Applicable taxable years covered (2022, 2023, and 2024): Consequently, the 2024 tax year is fully included in the small-business retroactive election alongside 2022 and 2023. An electing small business was required to apply its chosen Section 174A method consistently across all applicable taxable years (2022, 2023, and 2024) in which it paid or incurred domestic R&E expenditures, filing amended returns (or Administrative Adjustment Requests (AARs) for Bipartisan Budget Act partnerships) for any previously filed 2022–2024 returns and attaching a statement titled "FILED PURSUANT TO SECTION 3.03 OF REV. PROC. 2025-28".

Statutory deadline (July 6, 2026 — now closed) and deemed-election rules: Under Section 70302(f)(1)(A), the retroactive small-business election had to be made within one year after the July 4, 2025 enactment date. Because July 4, 2026 fell on a Saturday (and Independence Day legal holiday), Revenue Procedure 2025-28, Section 3.03(3) established that the election and all required amended returns or AARs had to be filed on or before July 6, 2026 (or, for any specific refund claim, before the expiration of the Section 6511 period of limitations on credit or refund, if earlier). Currency note: As of November 11, 2026, the July 6, 2026 window to make the retroactive small-business election has closed. Additionally, under Revenue Procedure 2025-28, Section 3.03(4), an eligible small business that deducted its 2024 domestic R&E expenditures on an original 2024 federal income tax return filed on or before November 15, 2025, was deemed to have made a valid Section 70302(f)(1) election for 2024 (provided it timely amended 2022 and 2023 if applicable).

2024 superseding return relief: For taxpayers (both small businesses and larger taxpayers) that had already filed an original 2024 return before the issuance of Revenue Procedure 2025-28 without requesting an extension, Revenue Procedure 2025-28, Section 8, granted an automatic 6-month extension of time (from the unextended original due date, where that due date fell before September 15, 2025) to file a superseding 2024 federal income tax return and furnish amended Schedules K-1, enabling eligible small businesses to claim immediate 2024 expensing under Section 174A on a superseding 2024 return and enabling other taxpayers to perfect 2024 Section 174 method changes.

Subsequent procedural coordination under Revenue Procedure 2026-32: Issued in September 2026 and effective for Forms 3115 filed after September 4, 2026, Revenue Procedure 2026-32 further modified Section 7 of Revenue Procedure 2025-23 (as previously modified by Revenue Procedure 2025-28) for the 2026 and 2027 filing seasons. Specifically, Revenue Procedure 2026-32 (1) coordinates modified Section 481(a) adjustments for taxpayers correcting impermissible accounting methods for 2022–2024 TCJA-period domestic SRE expenditures so that a net positive modified Section 481(a) adjustment is taken into account over the same 1-year or 2-year recovery period elected by the taxpayer under its Section 70302(f)(2) unamortized-balance recovery method (while allowing taxpayers with a negative modified Section 481(a) adjustment to choose a cut-off basis instead), and (2) removes the prior pre-January 1, 2026 sunset limitation on automatic accounting method changes for foreign R&E expenditures (Designated Change Number 274), extending automatic consent procedures for foreign R&E compliance to 2026 and subsequent tax years.

body.text: 4. Section 280C(c) coordination after 2024
The statutory relationship between Section 174 / Section 174A deductions and the Section 41 research credit shifted significantly between the 2022–2024 window and post-2024 years:

items: The 2022–2024 TCJA Section 280C(c) rule: For taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025 (unless an eligible small business made the retroactive Section 70302(f)(1) election), TCJA-amended Section 280C(c)(1) provided that the amount chargeable to capital account under Section 174 was reduced only to the extent that the Section 41(a) research credit exceeded the amount allowable as a Section 174 amortization deduction for that taxable year. Because a taxpayer's 10% first-year domestic amortization deduction (or cumulative amortization deduction) almost always exceeded its net Section 41 credit, most taxpayers during 2022–2024 suffered neither a reduction to their capitalized Section 174 basis nor a reduction to their Section 41 credit unless they affirmatively elected the Section 280C(c)(2) reduced credit.

Restoration of the dollar-for-dollar Section 280C(c) offset after 2024 (and for retroactive small-business years): Section 70302(c) of Public Law 119-21 amended Section 280C(c)(1) for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, to reinstate the pre-TCJA coordination rule: any deduction allowable under Section 174A(a) (or any amount charged to capital account under Section 174A(c) or Section 174) must be reduced by 100% of the amount of the Section 41(a) research credit determined for that taxable year. To avoid reducing the Section 174A deduction and having to track basis adjustments, a taxpayer may elect under Section 280C(c)(2) to claim a reduced Section 41 research credit (reduced by the maximum corporate tax rate of 21% under Section 11(b), yielding a net credit of 79% of the gross credit). Under Section 280C(c)(2)(C) and Revenue Procedure 2025-28, Section 2.05, the Section 280C(c)(2) reduced-credit election must be made on an original timely filed return (including extensions) and is irrevocable once made.

Retroactive Section 280C(c)(2) election/revocation for small businesses in 2022–2024: Because an eligible small business electing retroactive Section 174A expensing for 2022–2024 under Section 70302(f)(1)(A) also became retroactively subject to the post-OBBBA dollar-for-dollar Section 280C(c)(1) deduction reduction for 2022, 2023, and 2024, Section 70302(f)(1)(D) and Revenue Procedure 2025-28, Sections 4 and 5, allowed an electing small business to make a late Section 280C(c)(2) reduced-credit election—or revoke a previously made Section 280C(c)(2) election—for its 2022, 2023, and 2024 taxable years on amended returns filed on or before July 6, 2026 (which deadline has now passed).

body.text: 5. State conformity to the 2025 changes and impact on 2024 balances
State corporate and personal income tax treatment of 2024 R&E expenditures and post-2024 unamortized balance recoveries depends on each state's method of conforming to the Internal Revenue Code:

items: Rolling-conformity states (with selective decoupling): States with rolling IRC conformity automatically incorporate federal statutory amendments—including Section 174A and the Section 70302(f) transition rules—unless the state legislature enacts specific decoupling legislation. For example, Illinois operates as a rolling-conformity state under 35 ILCS 5/102. When the Illinois General Assembly enacted Senate Bill 1911 (Public Act 104-0453, signed December 12, 2025), Illinois specifically decoupled from the new federal 100% depreciation deduction for qualified production property under IRC Section 168(n) and modified its inclusion of net CFC tested income (NCTI), but did not decouple from IRC Section 174A or the Section 70302(f)(2) acceleration rules. Accordingly, Illinois conforms to federal Section 174A domestic expensing and the federal acceleration of unamortized 2022–2024 domestic R&E balances.

New York State and New York City — Statutory Decoupling: Pursuant to the enacted 2026–2027 New York State Budget and New York State Department of Taxation and Finance Important Notice N-26-1 (issued June 16, 2026, "Reporting certain depreciation and research and experimental expenditures for tax year 2025"), New York State and New York City decoupled from the federal OBBBA amendments to IRC Sections 174 and 174A (as well as the Section 70302(f)(2) unamortized balance acceleration rules), retroactive to taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2025. For New York State and New York City tax purposes, taxpayers must add back federal deductions claimed under IRC Section 174A(a) and Public Law 119-21 Section 70302(f)(2), and must instead compute New York R&E amortization adjustments under decoupled state rules (requiring Separate New York modification reporting on 2025 and subsequent returns).

Fixed-date (static) conformity states and pre-TCJA states — Nuanced Split: Approximately one-third of states enforce static IRC conformity tied to the Internal Revenue Code as of a specific date prior to July 4, 2025, meaning they do not automatically adopt Section 174A or the Section 70302(f) transition elections unless and until they update their statutory conformity dates.

States locked to TCJA §174 (post-2017, pre-July 4, 2025 conformity dates): Fixed-date states whose IRC conformity date falls between December 22, 2017, and July 3, 2025 (and that have not enacted a specific R&E exception) continue to mandate 5-year domestic and 15-year foreign amortization for 2024 and 2025 expenditures and do not recognize the federal Section 70302(f)(2) 1-year or 2-year acceleration of 2022–2024 balances.

States following pre-TCJA §174 or state-specific expensing overrides: Several major jurisdictions—most notably California (which generally conforms to the IRC as of January 1, 2015, under the California Revenue and Taxation Code), as well as states that enacted targeted R&E decoupling from TCJA Section 174 such as Georgia, Wisconsin, Indiana, and Tennessee, or states offering state-specific elections such as Alabama and Mississippi—never required mandatory 5-year TCJA capitalization for 2022–2024 domestic R&E in the first place. In those states, 2024 domestic R&E costs were already fully deducted on the 2024 state return, meaning there is no unamortized 2024 state balance to accelerate in 2025 or 2026 (requiring a state subtraction/addition modification to avoid double-deducting in 2025–2026 any 2022–2024 amounts accelerated on the federal return).

body.text: 6. Analysis: what this means for 2024 expenditures

items: 2024 as the final mandatory domestic capitalization vintage: Domestic R&E and software development expenditures paid or incurred in calendar year 2024 represent the final annual vintage subject to mandatory 5-year TCJA capitalization and the 10% first-year midpoint convention. For calendar-year taxpayers that did not (or could not) amend 2024 under the small-business rule, 90% of their 2024 domestic R&E spend entered 2025 as an unamortized capital balance.

Three recovery tracks for the remaining 90% of 2024 domestic costs: Under Section 70302(f)(2) and Revenue Procedure 2025-28, any taxpayer holding unamortized 2024 (and 2022–2023) domestic SRE balances can choose to (1) deduct 100% of the remaining unamortized balance in 2025, (2) deduct 50% in 2025 and 50% in 2026, or (3) leave the balance on its original 5-year schedule through 2029. Furthermore, under Revenue Procedure 2026-32, taxpayers filing Forms 3115 after September 4, 2026 to correct prior impermissible 2022–2024 domestic R&E methods must align any resulting net positive modified Section 481(a) adjustment with their elected 1-year or 2-year recovery schedule.

Permanent lock-in for 2024 foreign R&E costs: Foreign R&E and foreign software development costs incurred in 2024 received zero legislative relief under Public Law 119-21. The remaining 96.67% unamortized balance at the end of 2024 must continue to be amortized ratably over its 15-year midpoint schedule through 2039, and under amended Section 174(d), abandoning or disposing of the underlying foreign research property after May 12, 2025 cannot generate a loss deduction or reduce the amount realized.

Closure of the small-business retroactive window: For eligible small businesses meeting the $31,000,000 aggregated Section 448(c) gross receipts test, the statutory window to amend 2022, 2023, and 2024 returns to claim immediate Section 174A expensing closed on July 6, 2026. Small businesses that did not file amended returns (or qualify under the deemed-election or superseding-return rules of Revenue Procedure 2025-28) by July 6, 2026 must recover their unamortized 2022–2024 domestic balances prospectively using the Section 70302(f)(2) 1-year or 2-year acceleration options.

Multi-track federal and state amortization ledgers: Because states are split across at least three distinct regimes—rolling-conformity states that follow federal Section 174A and 2025–2026 acceleration (e.g., Illinois), states that decoupled from Section 174A and federal acceleration in 2026 (e.g., New York State and New York City under Notice N-26-1), and states that either remained on pre-TCJA expensing throughout 2022–2024 (e.g., California, Georgia, Wisconsin) or remain frozen on TCJA 5-year amortization—taxpayers must maintain separate federal and state R&E basis and amortization sub-ledgers for their 2024 expenditures.
